name: Herbst / twin-block functional appliance

lead: The Herbst (fixed) and Twin Block (removable) are functional appliances that hold the lower jaw forward in growing children and teenagers with a Class II overbite. The payoff is a corrected bite and a stronger chin and side profile; in looksmaxxing forums they are discussed as a way to advance a small or recessed lower jaw.

The appliance postures the lower jaw forward. Trials and meta-analyses report a modest average gain in lower-jaw length, around 1.5 to 2 mm or more versus controls, together with tooth movement. A review found about two-thirds of samples showed more than 2 mm of extra lengthening, with larger effects during puberty. How much is skeletal rather than dental remains debated.

paras: An orthodontist fits the Herbst, fixed with telescoping rods, or the Twin Block, a removable pair of acrylic plates, during the growth period, typically for months before further orthodontic treatment.

Reported effects include early soreness and chewing difficulty, speech changes with removable plates, and forward tilting of lower front teeth. A 2022 meta-analysis did not support forum claims that they recess the upper jaw.

angle.text: Herbst and Twin Block appliances hold the lower jaw forward in growing teens with an overbite, adding modest lower-jaw length and improving the side profile. Research is mostly in children; adult aesthetic use and home-made versions are not covered.

lead: The Herbst appliance and the Twin Block appliance are orthodontic devices known as functional appliances. They are used in growing children and adolescents with a Class II malocclusion, in which the upper front teeth sit forward of the lower ones and the lower jaw is often small or set back relative to the upper jaw. Both hold the lower jaw in a forward position so that the bite, the overjet (the horizontal gap between upper and lower front teeth) and, in some patients, the side profile of the lower face can change. The Herbst is fixed to the teeth and uses telescoping rods; the Twin Block is a removable pair of acrylic plates that guide the lower jaw forward when the patient bites together. [1][2]

For appearance, the appeal is the profile: a receding chin or a prominent upper lip can look more balanced when the lower jaw sits further forward. Studies that measured faces found that Herbst treatment tended to reduce the convexity of the hard- and soft-tissue profile, although long-term results varied between individuals. [3] Systematic reviews report that functional appliances correct overjet and molar relationship in growing patients through a mix of tooth movement and skeletal change. A review of 22 controlled studies found that about two-thirds of the treated samples gained more than 2 mm of extra lower-jaw length compared with untreated controls, with larger effects when treatment coincided with the pubertal growth period, while none of the four randomised trials in that review reported a clinically significant change in mandibular length. [4] A 2024 meta-analysis of 12 studies comparing the two appliances found slightly greater mandibular body lengthening with the Herbst and better molar and facial-convexity outcomes with the Twin Block. [5]

In looksmaxxing communities the devices are discussed as a way to advance a 'recessed' lower jaw in teenagers, alongside jaw surgery, fillers and over-the-counter mouthguards. Posters ask whether the appliances can be obtained cheaply or reproduced at home, whether they can be used without an overbite, and whether they recess the upper jaw. [6][7][8][9]

paras: The Herbst appliance is a fixed device. A stainless-steel framework is attached to the upper molars and lower premolars with bands or acrylic or cast splints, and a telescoping rod and tube on each side lets the patient open and close while the lower jaw stays advanced. Because it is bonded, it works around the clock without depending on the patient to put it in. [1]

The Twin Block consists of upper and lower acrylic plates with interlocking inclined bite planes; when the patient closes, the planes guide the lower jaw forward. Encyclopedic accounts describe an upper plate with an expansion screw, clasps on the back teeth and a ball-end clasp on the lower front teeth, worn full time apart from cleaning and contact sports. Because it is removable, results depend partly on how consistently it is worn. [2]

Both belong to a wider family that includes the Forsus fatigue resistance device, which is fixed to braces, Class II elastics (rubber bands), the Bionator and the Frankel appliance. Newer variants include mini-implant-supported and clear versions of the Twin Block, and clear aligners with functional features, which have been examined in recent trials and reviews. [10]

Wikipedia lists several Herbst design generations and relatives, including cast and acrylic-splint versions, ball joints for lateral movement, combinations with a palatal expander and later spring-type or cantilever bite jumpers. [1] A Cantilever Bite Jumper, Sabbagh spring and Powerscope are named as later fixed alternatives. [1]

For the Twin Block, Wikipedia describes the standard bite planes as set at about 70 degrees to the occlusal plane, with variants for Class II Division 2 and versions with headgear. [2] Because that article carries a notice that parts may be machine generated, its details are best read alongside the original papers listed below.

Functional appliances hold the lower jaw in a forward posture. Orthodontists describe the resulting change as a combination of tooth movement (upper teeth tipped back, lower teeth tipped forward), alveolar adaptation, and possible additional lower-jaw growth or remodelling at the joint. [11][12]

In Pancherz's 1982 study of 42 Class II Division 1 cases, 22 treated with the Herbst for 6 months and 20 controls, all treated cases reached a Class I bite, and the correction came about equally from skeletal and dental changes. Molar correction averaged 6.7 mm, mainly from a 2.2 mm increase in mandibular length plus movement of the upper and lower molars; overjet correction averaged 5.2 mm. [11] His earlier 1979 study of 20 growing boys, half treated for 6 months, likewise recorded greater-than-average mandibular growth, a slight reduction in the SNA angle (a measure of upper-jaw position) and reduced profile convexity. [12]
MRI and radiographic work has examined how the temporomandibular joint remodels during Herbst treatment in adolescents and young adults. [13]

Wikipedia's Herbst article states that starting at or just after the pubertal growth peak is associated with greater condylar growth, a more stable bite and less relapse, and that patients past the peak can still benefit from residual growth. [1] The Cozza review similarly found that supplementary mandibular growth appeared larger when treatment was timed at the pubertal peak. [4]

A cephalometric comparison of Twin Block treatment in 21 children treated around age 9 and 15 treated around age 13 concluded that treatment during or slightly after the onset of the pubertal growth peak produced a greater skeletal contribution, larger increases in mandibular length and ramus height, and more favourable condylar growth direction. [14] A 2023 randomised study with 36 patients compared Herbst IV treatment before and after puberty (mean ages about 9 and 16) using cone-beam CT and found significant differences between the groups only in horizontal measures of the lower jaw. [15]

Orthodontic descriptions of the Twin Block suggest it suits mild to moderate skeletal Class II cases with an average or low mandibular plane angle, and describe vertical growth patterns or already proclined lower incisors as situations in which other approaches may be preferred. [2] Adults with a Class II relationship are generally treated with other methods; the trials in this area enrol children and adolescents.

The Cozza systematic review (2006) searched literature from 1966 to 2005 and included 22 studies, four randomised trials and 18 controlled clinical trials, of quality from low to medium or high. Two-thirds of samples gained more than 2.0 mm of supplementary total mandibular length, but none of the four RCTs, three of them in prepubertal children, reported a clinically significant change. It calculated a coefficient of efficiency of 0.28 mm per month for the Herbst and 0.23 mm per month for the Twin Block. [4]

In the UK multicentre randomised trial of 174 children aged 8 to 10 with Class II Division 1 malocclusion, early Twin Block treatment was compared with no treatment over 15 months. It reduced overjet, corrected molar relationships and lowered the severity of the malocclusion; most of the change was dentoalveolar, with some favourable skeletal change that the authors said might not be clinically significant. [16]

A second trial from the same group randomised 215 patients aged 11 to 14 to the Herbst or the Twin Block. Failure to complete the functional phase was lower with the Herbst (12.9 percent) than with the Twin Block (33.6 percent); treatment time was similar, the Herbst needed about three more repair appointments, and skeletal and dental changes did not differ between appliances. Final occlusal results were better in girls than in boys, and the authors suggested that the Herbst's high cooperation rate could make it the appliance of choice for adolescents. [17]

The 2024 meta-analysis of 12 studies with 574 patients found a 1.44 mm greater increase in mandibular body length with the Herbst, more lower-incisor proclination with the Herbst, and greater improvement in molar relationship, posterior facial height and convexity angle with the Twin Block; SNA, SNB, ANB, overjet and overbite changes were similar. The authors concluded the Herbst may have advantages for mandibular bone movement and the Twin Block for facial aesthetics. [5]

A 2022 meta-analysis of nine studies (298 patients) compared the Herbst and Forsus with Class II elastics and found similar results for overbite, overjet, SNA and SNB, with the Herbst giving about 1.5 mm more mandibular length and 1.6 mm more ramus height. [10] A Cochrane review of orthodontic treatment for prominent upper front teeth in children and adolescents addresses early versus late timing and different braces.

Long-term profile results were examined by Pancherz and Anehus-Pancherz in 69 Class II Division 1 patients treated about 7 months with the Herbst and followed for 5 to 10 years: 49 kept a stable result and 20 relapsed. Treatment reduced hard- and soft-tissue profile convexity, but because of growth after treatment the long-term effects were described as variable and unpredictable. [3]

Recent randomised trials have tested a mini-implant-supported Twin Block against the conventional version, a modified clear Twin Block, and speech effects of a clear versus conventional Twin Block.  Soft-tissue profile change after functional therapy and head and cervical posture after Twin Block or Bionator treatment have also been studied.  A 2025 meta-analysis examined functional clear aligners for Class II correction in growing patients.  These studies were conducted in children and adolescents for medical orthodontic indications. No studies examined the appliances as a facial-aesthetic procedure in adults.

Reported effects of fixed functional appliances include early discomfort and difficulty chewing in the first weeks, and tooth movement such as lower-incisor proclination, which meta-analyses record as an outcome. Wikipedia also lists possible spacing in the upper arch. [1][5] Removable appliances can affect speech during the adjustment period, which a randomised trial has measured.  The Herbst trial recorded more repair appointments than the Twin Block, and the Twin Block trial arm recorded more patients who did not complete the functional phase. [17]

Wikipedia's Twin Block article lists posterior open bite when the patient does not hold the forward posture, and breakage of clasps among risks, and notes that some cases need a second phase of fixed braces. [2] Because the appliances are used in growing patients under orthodontic supervision, the documented effects in the literature relate to that setting.

Emil Herbst developed the appliance in the early 1900s according to encyclopedic accounts, and an 1886 editorial in The Dental Register already refers to Herbst's method. [18][1] It fell out of wide use and was reintroduced by Hans Pancherz, whose cephalometric studies from 1979 onward helped establish its modern use, and who later reviewed its biologic effects and clinical use. [1][12][11][19]

William J. Clark developed the Twin Block after treating a child whose upper incisor had been knocked out; according to Wikipedia, the first appliance was fitted on 7 September 1977 and the overjet fell from 9 mm to 4 mm within nine months. Clark's early blocks and their angulation were refined over time and the technique was published in 1982 and described in an overview in 1988. [2][20]

Randomised trials by a UK multicentre group in 2003 compared the Twin Block with no treatment and with the Herbst, giving the appliances some of their strongest comparative evidence. [16][17] Newer clear and implant-supported variants were being tested in trials around 2024 to 2025.

On looksmax.org, users in their mid-teens ask whether a Herbst can be obtained when cost is a barrier, and whether a home-made alternative exists. One reply recommends a commercial mouthguard-type device as a cheaper option, and the original poster expresses doubt about the seller's website. [7] Other threads ask whether the Herbst or Forsus can be used without an overbite, whether it recesses the upper jaw, and whether functional appliances affect the lower third of the face. [8][9][21]

Another thread has a teenager weighing a Herbst against filler for a profile they describe as recessed, alongside plans for later surgery. [22] One thread asserts that orthodontists using Herbst appliances and rubber bands stunt upper-jaw growth. [6] The wider community conversation treats growth-stage orthodontics as a window that closes in adulthood, when surgical options are discussed instead.

Related options discussed alongside functional appliances include other bite-correcting devices such as the Forsus and Class II elastics, headgear for upper-jaw growth modification, jaw surgery (mandibular advancement) for adults, chin implants or genioplasty, and filler for the chin and jawline. [10][22]

timeline.event: An editorial in The Dental Register discusses Herbst's method. [18]
William Clark fits the first Twin Block-type appliance, according to Wikipedia. [2]
Pancherz publishes a cephalometric study of bite jumping with the Herbst appliance in 20 boys. [12]
Pancherz reports mechanisms of Class II correction with the Herbst in 42 cases; Clark's first Twin Block paper appears. [11][20]
The Twin Block technique is described in the American Journal of Orthodontics and Dentofacial Orthopedics.
Pancherz and Anehus-Pancherz report 5 to 10 year facial-profile follow-up of 69 Herbst-treated patients. [3]
Baccetti and colleagues publish a cephalometric study on treatment timing for Twin Block therapy. [14]
UK multicentre randomised trials of the Twin Block versus no treatment and of Herbst versus Twin Block are published. [16][17]
Cozza and colleagues publish a systematic review of 22 studies on mandibular changes from functional appliances. [4]
Meta-analysis compares Herbst, Forsus and Class II elastics in nine studies. [10]
A meta-analysis compares Twin Block and Herbst outcomes in 12 studies with 574 patients. [5]
